summary:
Blink 102 lets anyone type the name or coordinates of a star and watch NASA SPHEREx images of that spot change over time, like the blink comparator that found Pluto in 1930, but in 102 infrared colours.

It finds every SPHEREx exposure released for that position (Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3, three to four sky passes about six months apart), reads only the pixels needed from each 65 MB file, lines them up on one grid, and stacks them by date. Moving stars step across the frames; variable stars brighten and fade.

Because SPHEREx sees 102 colours, users can slide through the infrared, watch the coldest brown dwarf known appear only at the long end, and click any dot to get its spectrum, its brightness history and its measured motion from every single exposure.

On the challenge's test targets the measured motions match the catalogues: Barnard's Star 10.41 ± 0.46″/yr (catalogue 10.39), eps Indi B 4.59 ± 0.04″/yr (4.68). It turns brand-new NASA data into something anyone can explore, and something citizen scientists can search.
details:
What it does

  • Type a star's name or coordinates (with suggestions as you type) and see that patch of sky blink between SPHEREx's sky passes. Object positions are moved forward by their proper motion: the challenge's coordinates for WISE 0855 date from about 2010, and it has since moved 2.2′, so the tool recentres on where it is now.
  • Choose which of SPHEREx's 102 infrared colours go into the picture with one slider, or press Sweep to slide through all of them. By default every wavelength is drawn in its own colour on one brightness scale, so a dot's colour is the real shape of its spectrum: ordinary stars look white, cold brown dwarfs glow red to magenta.
  • Click any dot to measure it in every exposure: its spectrum (with a blackbody fit and the depth of the water and methane bands), its brightness over time (with a period search for variable stars), and its proper motion fitted to the centre of light after removing parallax.
  • Difference mode, a flags overlay showing pixels SPHEREx marked as unreliable, Follow mode (hold a moving object still while the sky moves) and All-dates stacking for faint objects.
  • Gaia DR3, SIMBAD and CatWISE objects drawn where they should be on each date. A scan lists everything in the field that moves and flags movers that are in no catalogue.
  • Shareable links that reopen the exact view, an embed mode for other websites, image and video export, a 40-second guided tour, and a Plate theme that shows the sky as black stars on paper.

How it works

  1. Search: IRSA's Simple Image Access service lists every SPHEREx exposure covering the position (collections spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3, wide and deep). Nothing is hard-coded, so new weekly releases appear automatically.
  2. Reading: each exposure is a 65 MB file. A small Python function reads a few hundred kilobytes of it from NASA's public SPHEREx bucket on AWS using HTTP range requests: the header, the rows around the target, the matching rows of the compressed flag layer, and the wavelength table.
  3. Alignment: each cutout is resampled with Astropy's WCS (including the SIP distortion) onto one north-up grid; the sky background is fitted and removed; SPHEREx's flag bits are folded into plain categories.
  4. Everything else runs instantly in the browser: stacking by date and colour, the blink, photometry, spectra, light curves, motion fits and the scan.

Results on the test targets (computed by the same code that runs on the page; measured vs catalogue)

  • Barnard's Star: 10.41 ± 0.46″/yr vs 10.39″/yr.
  • eps Indi B: 4.59 ± 0.04″/yr vs 4.68″/yr; methane band 80% deep, as expected for T-type brown dwarfs.
  • WISE 0855−0714: detected only at 3.8–5.0 µm, about 500 µJy (W2 ≈ 480 µJy), on the predicted track; found blind by the motion scan from the challenge's old coordinates.
  • RW Aur: brightness changes of 0.7 mag at 3.8–5.0 µm between passes (irregular variable).
  • R Dra: 1.7 mag swings; period 245 ± 61 days from two cycles (Mira, about 246 days).
  • Luhman 16: 2.79 ± 0.08″/yr vs 2.79″/yr.
  • 2MASS 0415−0935: 2.28 ± 0.16″/yr vs 2.26″/yr; methane band 96% deep.

Fluxes agree with 2MASS to within 5% for unsaturated field stars. Barnard's Star, RW Aur and R Dra are too bright for SPHEREx; the tool says so and measures them from their unsaturated outer light. These limits are listed in the README.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve. Most known brown dwarfs near the Sun were confirmed with blink tools like WiseView, many by volunteers. SPHEREx adds 102 colours, so a cold object can be recognised by its colour as well as its motion. We hope Blink 102 lets students, amateurs and citizen scientists explore SPHEREx on day one of each new release, and helps someone find a cold world no one has catalogued yet.

Tools. Python (Astropy, NumPy, SciPy) for the data functions; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface, with no framework; Aladin Lite for the wider sky view; hosted on Vercel. Source code and full documentation: https://github.com/shrestha-droid/blink-102

Use of AI. We directed Claude (Anthropic) as our engineering tool. Under our direction it wrote the code for the website and the data functions, researched the SPHEREx file formats and documentation, drafted the design, ran the checks we asked for, drafted the README and this text, and edited our demo video from real screen recordings of the tool. Our team chose the challenge, decided what to build and what to cut, reviewed every stage on the live site, and is responsible for the results. No image or footage was generated by AI: every picture of the sky comes from NASA SPHEREx data, and the AI-assisted video edit carries a watermark. The video's quiet background sound (a low tone and clicks, no music) was synthesized with AI assistance. AI use is also described in the README and in the header of every source file.
